scenario_stem:
Saltrunner Surfboards is a sole trader business owned by Marco Deleanu, shaping bespoke surfboards in a small coastal workshop in Country X for 6 years. Saltrunner employs 3 skilled shapers and produces 220 custom boards a year, each hand-shaped over 9 hours and sold at $1,450, generating annual revenue of $319,000. Fixed costs are $4,000 a month and materials cost $180 per board.

A national surf retailer has offered a 2-year contract for 800 identical boards a year at $620 each. Marco could accept by introducing batch production with 2 Computer-Aided Design templates and $55,000 of new machinery, or he could refuse and keep shaping one-off boards for his loyal custom customers. He must decide before the retailer's order deadline on 30 September.

scenario_stem:
Elmsworth & Cross Watchmakers Ltd is a private limited company founded 12 years ago by two horologists in Country X, employing 9 master watchmakers and selling hand-built watches at $9,500 each. Elmsworth sold 240 watches last year, generating revenue of $2.28 million; each watch takes 30 hours to assemble and regulate, and waiting lists run to 7 months. Elmsworth's clients are collectors who value heritage and discretion.

The owners could launch a $1,800 everyday automatic watch made on a small flow production line costing $900,000 with 12 new assembly staff, or stay exclusively with hand-built watches and raise prices by 15% to clear the 7-month backlog and shorten waiting lists. The board meets in December to decide between the two plans.

questions.question_text: State two disadvantages of flow production.
questions.model_answer: It requires very high capital investment in machinery [1]; a breakdown stops the whole production line [1].

knowledge_max_2: flow production needs very high capital investment
in flow production one breakdown halts the whole line

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why job production suits Elmsworth & Cross's luxury watches.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Job production makes one-off items to exact specification [k], suiting the 30 hours of individual assembly and regulation each $9,500 watch requires [app]. Reason 2: Job production supports premium craftsmanship and pricing [k], letting 9 master watchmakers sell genuinely hand-built watches to clients who wait 7 months [app].

knowledge_max_2: job production makes one-offs to individual specification
job production enables premium craftsmanship and pricing
application_max_2: 30 hours per watch at $9,500 each
9 master watchmakers; 7-month waiting lists

questions.question_text: Explain two risks to Elmsworth & Cross of launching the $1,800 flow-made watch.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: The $900,000 line with 12 new assembly staff is a heavy fixed commitment [k], and if the everyday watch disappoints, the cost cannot easily be repaid at $1,800 each, roughly a fifth of the luxury price [app], so one weak launch damages cash flow [an]. Problem 2: A cheaper line can blur exclusivity [k], diluting the hand-built reputation that supports $2.28 million of annual sales [app], so loyal collectors may question what the brand now stands for [an].

knowledge_max_2: flow lines need large fixed capital commitments that are hard to exit
product-line extensions can dilute brand positioning
application_max_2: $900,000 line and 12 staff vs a $1,800 selling price
reputation underpins $2.28 million annual sales at $9,500
analysis_max_2: low selling price makes recouping the line slow
brand dilution could erode the core luxury customer base

questions.question_text: Do you think Elmsworth & Cross Watchmakers should launch the $1,800 flow-made watch rather than only raise prices by 15%? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Raising prices by 15% would grow revenue without new risk [k], since 240 watches at $10,925 would bring about $2.62 million, roughly $342,000 more a year [app], while protecting the exclusive hand-built positioning [an]. However, the $1,800 watch could reach far more buyers than 240 a year [k], and the $900,000 line with 12 new assembly staff could open a larger market and spread brand awareness [app], building long-term demand beyond the waiting list [an]. Overall, Elmsworth & Cross should raise prices and hold the flow line under review [eval], because exclusivity underpins the $9,500 price, and $342,000 of low-risk extra revenue beats betting $900,000 on an unproven mass market [eval].

knowledge_max_2: price rises lift revenue with no capital risk
a flow-made entry range can expand market reach at scale
application_max_2: 240 watches at $10,925 = about $2.62 million, +$342,000 a year
$900,000 line, 12 staff, $1,800 selling price vs $9,500 luxury price
analysis_max_2: low-risk margin gain versus scalable but unproven demand
brand exclusivity versus audience growth
evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation tied to the figures and the waiting-list position

scenario_stem:
Kilnworth Ceramics Ltd is a private limited company in Country X employing 36 production workers and 4 packers making ceramic tableware for hotel groups and restaurant chains. Last week the factory produced 27,000 plates and bowls on one 8-hour shift, five days a week; labour productivity was 750 pieces per worker. Sales have grown steadily for three years, and two hotel groups want 40,500 pieces a week next year.

Kilnworth could add a second 8-hour shift with 36 new workers at $485 a week each to reach 54,000 pieces a week, or install a new shuttle kiln for $260,000 to raise productivity to 1,150 pieces per worker. Both options would begin after the January delivery window, and the cheaper option must be chosen by February.

questions.question_text: Calculate the labour productivity of Kilnworth's production workers last week. Show your working.
questions.model_answer: Labour productivity = output / workers = 27,000 / 36 = 750 pieces per worker per week [2].

knowledge_max_2: labour productivity = output / number of workers
27,000 / 36 = 750 pieces per worker

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Kilnworth of installing the new shuttle kiln rather than adding a second shift.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: The kiln raises productivity per worker [k], lifting output from 750 to 1,150 pieces per worker with the same 36 production workers [app]. Benefit 2: The kiln avoids recurring shift wages [k], saving 36 x $485 = $17,460 a week compared with a second shift [app].

knowledge_max_2: machinery raises output per worker
machinery avoids recurring wage costs of extra shifts
application_max_2: 750 to 1,150 pieces per worker with 36 production workers
36 x $485 = $17,460 a week saved versus a second shift

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Kilnworth may face if it adds a second shift with 36 new workers.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: A second shift roughly doubles labour cost [k], adding 36 x $485 = $17,460 a week to the payroll before overtime and supervision [app], squeezing margins on price-sensitive hotel contracts [an]. Problem 2: New workers need training and quality checks [k], and with only 4 packers to handle 54,000 pieces a week [app], breakages and delivery delays could hit both hotel groups [an].

knowledge_max_2: a second shift adds permanent recurring labour cost
new workers require training and quality supervision
application_max_2: 36 x $485 = $17,460 a week extra payroll
only 4 packers for 54,000 pieces a week
analysis_max_2: margins squeezed on price-sensitive hotel contracts
packing bottleneck causes breakages and late deliveries

questions.question_text: Do you think Kilnworth Ceramics should install the new shuttle kiln rather than add a second shift? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: The $260,000 kiln would lift productivity to 1,150 pieces per worker [k], so the existing 36 workers make 41,400 pieces a week and cover the hotel groups' 40,500 target [app], avoiding $17,460 a week of second-shift wages [an]. However, a second shift with 36 new workers would reach 54,000 pieces a week [k], giving spare capacity if both hotel groups expand beyond 40,500 [app], whereas the kiln's 41,400 leaves little headroom [an]. Overall, Kilnworth should install the kiln [eval], because a second shift would cost about $907,920 a year in wages against a one-off $260,000, and confirmed demand is only 40,500 pieces [eval].

knowledge_max_2: capital investment raises productivity without recurring wages
a second shift doubles capacity but doubles labour cost
application_max_2: kiln: 1,150 x 36 = 41,400 pieces per week, covering 40,500 needed
second shift: 54,000 pieces a week; 36 x $485 = $17,460 a week (~$907,920 a year)
analysis_max_2: headroom for growth versus cheaper one-off outlay
recurring wage cost versus capital outlay
evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation tied to confirmed demand of 40,500 pieces
